status: proposal; not applied to the atlas
scope: Evidence for three person-to-Canadian-group teaching edges. The atlas covers 1920–2000. Directed edges evidenced only by post-2000 work are deferred, following GRAPH-FORMAT.md revision 1.128.
phd_context_source: data/extension-2026/canadian-historiography-groups-request-2026-10-12/answers/person-entry-links.json (1,303 Canadian History PhDs, 2009–2026). The figures give context; they do not show who influenced whom.
access_notes: Érudit PDFs for Labour/Le Travailleur were read on 2026-10-13. Érudit intermittently served an Anubis bot check, and Project MUSE, the York journal sites (Histoire sociale, Left History), De Gruyter and H-Net blocked automated reading. edges.relationship: Canadian new labour historians draw on Thompson's class and culture, and critics contest whether it fits Canada
edges.map_label: Thompson and Canadian new labour history
edges.evidence_note: Both sides of the 1981 Labour/Le Travailleur exchange, read in full, treat Thompson as the reference point for Canadian new labour history. Kealey (pp. 82–83) calls The Making 'probably the most influential piece of historical writing in the English language published since 1960' and says 'Thompson's influence is our concern'. In North America, critics attack 'works which have associated themselves with Thompson's method'. He concedes (p. 87) that users of British social history must show that it applies 'to the Canadian context'. Bercuson (pp. 97–98) says Canadian new labour historians 'follow the thinking of E.P. Thompson' and 'lean to the British experience', studying culture 'in the Thompson sense'. Palmer, he says, echoes Thompson. Bercuson objects (p. 108) that 'even if Thompson is right about England, his concepts do not necessarily apply anywhere else'. McNaught's 1981 CHR title frames the decade as 'E. P. Thompson vs Harold Logan'. Palmer, a leading new labour historian, wrote a book on Thompson (1981). Limits: this is testimony from the debate about Thompson's influence, not a reading of Palmer's or Kealey's monographs. Gutman is named alongside Thompson throughout, and the claim is about a resource and reference point, not adoption of one theory. PhD context: 38 of 106 Canadian History PhDs (2009–2026) citing Thompson engage this field (36%, lift 1.64). This is weaker than Scott's or Hall's pairings, but the pre-2000 evidence is the strongest of the three edges.
edges.overlap_with_existing: edge_886 (marx → cdn_working_class) already carries the label 'Thompsonian class and culture in Canadian labour history' and the map label 'Thompson and the new labour history' on McNaught and Kealey. If this edge is accepted, edge_886 should be relabelled to Marxist class analysis generally (e.g. 'Marxist class analysis in the new labour history'), or its Thompson wording moved here, so that two arrows do not tell the same story.

recommendation.reason: Two pre-2000 Canadian texts read in full name Thompson's influence on Canadian new labour history from opposite sides, with page-located quotations. The direction (Thompson → field) and kind (contribution, not influence on every practitioner) are supported.

edges.relationship: Scott's theory of gender is weighed in Canadian debates over discourse, experience and gender history
edges.map_label: Scott's gender theory in Canadian debates
edges.evidence_note: Valverde's 1990 review essay in Labour/Le Travail, read in full, treats Scott's Gender and the Politics of History (with Riley) as a key work in 'the controversy about discourse theory'. She notes that poststructuralism had a 'bad reputation … among socialists and feminists (in English Canada, at least)' and that 'in Canada' the debate was posed as 'a yes-or-no question'. She concludes that Scott 'deserves to be carefully read even by those who find some of its more polemical claims hard to swallow'. Pierson's 1991 essay on Canadian women's history opens on the turn to deconstruction, with Scott's theorising of gender as its most acclaimed example (opening read). Reference lists show Scott cited by Linda Kealey (1992), Pierson (1992) and Parr's 1995 CHR essay on gender history (OpenAlex metadata; texts unread). Limits: the evidence shows engagement and debate, not adoption. Valverde is sympathetic but critical. Palmer's Descent into Discourse (1990) is a Canadian critique of the linguistic turn, but its treatment of Scott was not checked here. The 1995–96 Left History exchange is title-level and is not evidence that names Scott. PhD context: 64 of 120 Canadian History PhDs citing Scott engage this field (53%, lift 2.12); 39 engage childhood and youth (lift 3.21), and 49 working-class history (lift 1.87).
edges.overlap_with_existing: edge_840 (cdn_women_gender → gender, 'Canadian debates over gender as a category') already cites Pierson 1991 and Scott 1986. The new edge is distinct: it joins the person entry to the Canadian field, which the family view needs to show Scott. Keep both; the evidence notes should cross-refer.

recommendation.reason: Two pre-2000 Canadian texts were read at the relevant passages (Valverde in full; Pierson's opening) and explicitly engage Scott's theory in a Canadian frame, with three further pre-2000 citations at reference-list level. 'Contribution' is used in the format's sense of a conceptual resource that was debated; if editors prefer, 'comparison' would understate the documented engagement.

edges.relationship: Family Fortunes and Canadian studies of gender, family and middle-class formation
edges.map_label: Family Fortunes and Canadian gender history
edges.evidence_note: No pre-2000 Canadian women's or gender history text was found that explicitly engages Family Fortunes at a checked passage. Darroch (1999), an Ontario historical-sociology article, cites Family Fortunes in its deposited references; its abstract qualifies the 'domestic revolution' account of middle-class formation for Ontario, but it does not name Davidoff and Hall and it belongs to family history. Parr reviewed Hall's White, Male and Middle Class in the CHR (1993), and Morgan reviewed Davidoff's Worlds Between in Histoire sociale (1998). Both are metadata only: the reviews were unreadable behind bot checks. Morgan's Public Men and Virtuous Women (1996) works the same public/private terrain, but no checked page links it to Davidoff and Hall. OpenAlex citation data show no pre-2001 CHR, Histoire sociale or Labour/Le Travail article citing Family Fortunes, though coverage of 1990s Canadian journals is incomplete. PhD context: 58 of 108 Canadian History PhDs citing Hall engage this field (54%, lift 2.13); Davidoff 31 of 49 (63%, lift 2.51). The strong present-day co-citation may reflect later uptake: Hall's Civilising Subjects (2002) and work on gender and empire, such as Perry's On the Edge of Empire (2001).

recommendation.reason: There is no checked pre-2000 passage in which a Canadian women's or gender historian engages Family Fortunes or Hall. The available pre-2000 items are metadata-level reviews and one family-history abstract whose citation of Family Fortunes is visible only in its reference list. The edge as drafted (an undirected comparison) is for a later extension release once Parr's 1993 review, Morgan's 1996 introduction or 1998 review, or a 1990s separate-spheres article is read. A contribution supported only by post-2000 publications (e.g. Perry 2001; Hall 2002; Christie, ed., Households of Faith, 2002) requires the extension workflow; a checked 1990s passage could support an ordinary in-period edge.

considered_not_proposed.note: The framework itself dates from McKay's 2000 prospectus (lof_mckay_2000). Its OpenAlex reference list (74 matched works, checked 2026-10-13) includes no work by Hall or Davidoff. The PhD pairing (45 of 108, 42%, lift 2.48) reflects post-2000 work, probably the Constant and Ducharme volume (2009) and Hall's imperial histories. Revisit only with a post-2000 works-and-claims release.

The PhD pairing is stronger than Hall's (31 of 49, lift 2.51), and Morgan reviewed Davidoff's Worlds Between in Histoire sociale (1998, metadata only). Any Family Fortunes edge should treat the two authors together, as edge_757 does.

ep_thompson__cdn_working_class.use_in_this_edge: Principal evidence: a founding Canadian new labour historian names Thompson's influence as the issue and acknowledges the obligation to test it on Canadian evidence.

proposed_verification_addendum.note: Pages 67–68 and 82–87 read closely with their footnotes; the rest skimmed by keyword (Érudit PDF, id.erudit.org/iderudit/llt7cri01; Critiques section, pp. 67–94, which also confirms the end page the existing record inferred). p. 67: the moment for evaluating the labour history of the 1960s–70s has arrived, signalled in Britain by the confrontation of “Althusserian structuralism and Thompsonian ‘culturalist’ or ‘socialist-humanist’ history”. p. 68: names McNaught’s forthcoming “E.P. Thompson vs. Harold Logan” as making “only too clear the eminently political nature of the emerging debate”. pp. 82–83: The Making of the English Working Class “has probably been the most influential piece of historical writing in the English language published since 1960”; “For our purposes, Thompson’s influence is our concern”; in North America “the critics are most often anti-Marxists attacking works which have associated themselves with Thompson’s method”. p. 87: quotes Bercuson (1979) accusing working-class historians of paying “due obeisance to E.P. Thompson, the guru” and “shoehorning their subjects into a Thompsonian mould”, and concedes that those “who utilize the insights of British … social history” must “demonstrate convincingly that they apply to the Canadian context”. The footnotes to these pages were read; the rest of the essay was skimmed by keyword only.

ep_thompson__cdn_working_class.use_in_this_edge: A critic's testimony that Canadian new labour history followed Thompson, with the critic's limit stated.

proposed_verification_addendum.note: Full text read (Érudit PDF, id.erudit.org/iderudit/llt7cri02, pp. 95–112). p. 97: Canadian practitioners of the new labour history “follow the thinking of E.P. Thompson in Britain, Herbert Gutman in the United States, and others in applying the culturalist approach to Canadian experience”; “Palmer, echoing E.P. Thompson, regards culture and conflict as ‘complementary processes’” (citing A Culture in Conflict, p. xii, which was not itself checked). p. 98: in Canada new labour historians “stand in the middle but so far tend to lean to the British experience. They study working-class culture for the explanation and definition they believe it offers in the Thompson sense”. p. 108: “Even if Thompson is right about England, his concepts do not necessarily apply anywhere else.” A critic’s characterization, not a self-description.

ep_thompson__cdn_working_class.use_in_this_edge: Title-level only: the 1981 CHR review essay frames the decade as 'E. P. Thompson vs Harold Logan'. Argument known only through Finkel (wcreq_finkel_2021).

ep_thompson__cdn_working_class.title: Bryan D. Palmer, “Homage to Edward Thompson, Part I,” Labour/Le Travailleur 32 (1993): 10–72; “Part II,” 33 (1994): 13–68.
ep_thompson__cdn_working_class.citation: Bryan D. Palmer, “Homage to Edward Thompson, Part I,” Labour/Le Travailleur 32 (1993): 10–72; “Homage to Edward Thompson, Part II,” Labour/Le Travailleur 33 (1994): 13–68, doi:10.2307/25143788.

verification.note: Érudit PDFs (llt32ob01, llt33art01) opened; Érudit citation gives pp. 10–72 and 13–68; Crossref record for Part II (doi:10.2307/25143788). Read: Part I opening, p. 10: Thompson's histories “occupy a special and influential place”, alongside “a nagging denigration of his accomplishments”; a footnote lists Greg Kealey's obituary in the St. John's Evening Telegram (5 September 1993). Keyword search of both parts found biography and political history, not an account of Thompson's reception in Canadian labour history (except Queen's University seminars in 1988 and a Kingston theatre visit). Shows that the Canadian Committee on Labour History's journal gave Thompson a two-part obituary of some 120 pages; it is not evidence of his influence on Canadian research.

ep_thompson__cdn_working_class.scope_note: The Canadian labour history journal's two-part obituary of Thompson (opening read; supplementary).

joan_wallach_scott__cdn_women_gender.title: Mariana Valverde, “Poststructuralist Gender Historians: Are We Those Names?” Labour/Le Travail 25 (1990): 227–36.
joan_wallach_scott__cdn_women_gender.citation: Mariana Valverde, “Poststructuralist Gender Historians: Are We Those Names?” Labour/Le Travail 25 (1990): 227–36 (review essay on Denise Riley, ‘Am I That Name?’ (1988), and Joan Wallach Scott, Gender and the Politics of History (1988)); doi:10.2307/25143354.

verification.note: Full text read (Érudit PDF, Review Essays, pp. 227–236); Crossref and OpenAlex records (OpenAlex abstract = opening paragraphs). p. 227: reviews Riley and Scott as “two key works” in “the controversy about discourse theory”; “Some of Joan Scott's essays are biting attacks on empiricism, particularly as practiced by historians of women”; ‘experience’ was “the central category in the pioneering work of E.P. Thompson”. p. 228: poststructuralism's “bad reputation … among socialists and feminists (in English Canada, at least)”. p. 233: “Scott's work deserves to be carefully read even by those who find some of its more polemical claims hard to swallow”; she may exaggerate what Foucault and Derrida can contribute and in “her reaction against both Thompsonian and empiricist traditions”. Note on p. 233: “In Canada, the debate about theory and discourse, such as it is, seems to be posed as a yes-or-no question”. Valverde (York University) writes as a participant; this is a sympathetic but critical review, not a survey of Canadian practice.

joan_wallach_scott__cdn_women_gender.scope_note: A Toronto feminist scholar's review essay of Scott (and Riley) in the Canadian labour history journal, placing the discourse debate in English Canada (full text).

joan_wallach_scott__cdn_women_gender.use_in_this_edge: Existing check: opening text names Scott's theorising of 'gender' as the most acclaimed example of feminist historians' turn to deconstruction and discourse analysis. Already used in edge_840.
Parr's CHR state-of-the-field essay on gender history cites Scott (reference list only).

proposed_verification_addendum.note: OpenAlex reference list for the article (W2118812311; 33 matched references) includes three works by Scott: 'The Evidence of Experience' (1991), 'Deconstructing Equality-versus-Difference' and 'The Campaign against Political Correctness' (1992), alongside Riley, Canning and Sonya Rose on gender history and women's history. Reference-matching metadata only; how Parr uses them was not read.

catherine_hall__cdn_women_gender.title: Gordon Darroch, “Domestic Revolution and Cultural Formation in Nineteenth-Century Ontario, Canada,” History of the Family 4, no. 4 (1999): 427–45.
catherine_hall__cdn_women_gender.citation: Gordon Darroch, “Domestic Revolution and Cultural Formation in Nineteenth-Century Ontario, Canada,” The History of the Family 4, no. 4 (1999): 427–445.

verification.note: Abstract read (OpenAlex): close historical studies of the rise of the urban middle-class family “located the core of middle-class formation in a virtual domestic revolution”; a review of Ontario evidence “suggests alternatively” that the roots of middle-class family culture were “more widespread, and are more deeply buried”. The Crossref deposited reference list (74 references) includes Davidoff and Hall, Family Fortunes (1987) and Ryan, Cradle of the Middle Class (1981). The abstract does not name Davidoff and Hall; which studies it means is inferred from the references. Article unread. Darroch is a historical sociologist; the journal is international, and this is family and middle-class history rather than Canadian women's history.

catherine_hall__cdn_women_gender.scope_note: An Ontario historical-sociology study that qualifies the domestic-revolution account of middle-class formation and cites Family Fortunes (abstract and reference list).
